questions.q: Ships' navigators have long used the Mercator Projection. Which feature of this projection makes it useful for navigation?
questions.a: It preserves shape and direction.
o: It preserves shape and direction.
It shows every country at its true size.
It balances size and shape distortions.
It shows the areas near the poles without distortion.

questions.q: (a) What is a map projection? (b) Who is a cartographer?
questions.a: (a) A map projection is the process of showing the Earth on a flat surface. (b) A cartographer is a person who draws or produces maps.
s: (a) Map projection: the process of showing the Earth on a flat surface
(b) Cartographer: a person who draws or produces maps

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Every flat map of the world has some distortion.
Reason (R): The Earth is an oblate spheroid, and its curved surface cannot be laid flat without tearing, just as an orange peel cannot.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: A Class 8 quiz team notices that Greenland looks about as big as Africa on one wall map but much smaller on a second wall map. (a) Name the projection on which Greenland looks as big as Africa. (b) Explain why that projection makes Greenland look so large. (c) Which of the two maps should the team trust more when comparing the sizes of countries, and why?
questions.a: (a) The Mercator Projection. (b) The Mercator Projection keeps shape and direction but greatly distorts size near the poles, so a land near the pole such as Greenland is shown much bigger than it is. (c) The Robinson Projection, because it is a compromise that balances size and shape distortions; it is still not perfect, since every map has some distortion.
s: (a) Names the Mercator Projection
(b) Mercator greatly distorts size near the poles, so Greenland is shown enlarged
(c) Chooses the Robinson Projection because it balances size and shape distortions (no map is free of distortion)

questions.q: A television news show puts up a Mercator world map and tells viewers, 'As you can see, Greenland is bigger than India.' Write a four-step correction for the show: (1) why no flat map can be free of distortion; (2) what the Mercator Projection keeps right and what it gets wrong; (3) the true size relation between Greenland and India; (4) what the show should do instead before comparing sizes or giving exact positions.
questions.a: (1) The Earth is an oblate spheroid; like an orange peel, its surface cannot be laid flat without tearing, so every map projection has some distortion and every map is a compromise. (2) The Mercator Projection preserves shape and direction, which makes it good for navigation, but it greatly distorts size near the poles. (3) Greenland looks larger than India on the Mercator map, but in fact Greenland is smaller than India. (4) The show should look at more than one projection, such as the Robinson Projection, which balances size and shape distortions; for precise positions, professionals use maps based on latitude and longitude coordinates.
s: (1) The Earth is an oblate spheroid that cannot be flattened without tearing, so every map distorts
(2) Mercator preserves shape and direction but greatly distorts size near the poles
(3) Greenland is in fact smaller than India
(4) Compare multiple projections such as the Robinson, and use latitude-longitude coordinates for precise positions

questions.a: About 71 per cent

questions.q: True or False? 'The oceans give us almost half the oxygen we breathe, and tiny organisms such as plankton make this possible.' Give the verdict and one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. Plankton are microscopic organisms that have chlorophyll and use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make food; through them the oceans give us almost half the oxygen we breathe.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: plankton have chlorophyll and use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make food, which is how the oceans give almost half our oxygen

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What shape are the very deep areas of the seafloor called trenches? (b) Which is the deepest trench? (c) Name its deepest section and say how far below sea level it reaches.
questions.a: (a) Trenches are very deep, V-shaped areas of the seafloor. (b) The Mariana Trench. (c) The Challenger Deep, which reaches over 11,000 metres below sea level.
s: (a) V-shaped
(b) The Mariana Trench
(c) The Challenger Deep, over 11,000 metres below sea level

questions.q: Answer each part in one or two lines. (a) Name the five oceans. (b) Which ocean does the chapter's map of oceans describe as the smallest and shallowest, covered with sea ice? (c) Which ocean encircles Antarctica? (d) What does a cold current carry, and in which direction? (e) A seaside town in Western Europe is warmer than other places at the same latitude. Name the current that makes it warmer.
questions.a: (a) The Indian, the Pacific, the Arctic, the Atlantic and the Southern Oceans. (b) The Arctic Ocean. (c) The Southern Ocean. (d) A cold current brings cold water from the poles toward the equator. (e) The Gulf Stream, a warm current that flows north from near the Equator through the Atlantic Ocean towards Western Europe.
s: (a) Names all five oceans: Indian, Pacific, Arctic, Atlantic, Southern
(b) The Arctic Ocean
(c) The Southern Ocean
(d) Cold water, from the poles toward the equator
(e) The Gulf Stream

questions.q: A farmer in the Gangetic Plains of Bihar lives hundreds of kilometres from any sea, yet the chapter says the distant Southern Indian Ocean influences the monsoon there. Which role of the oceans, as the chapter describes it, best explains how an ocean can affect rain so far inland?
questions.a: Oceans add moisture to the air, forming clouds and rainfall.
o: Oceans add moisture to the air, forming clouds and rainfall.
Oceans hold 97 per cent of the Earth's water.
Oceans give us almost half the oxygen we breathe.
The ocean floor has mountains, valleys and plains.

questions.q: A travel blogger notes that in winter a seaside town in the United Kingdom is milder than a town at the same latitude on a coast that no warm current reaches. (a) Name the current responsible and say where it starts. (b) Using the chapter's description of warm currents, explain why it makes the UK town milder.
questions.a: (a) The Gulf Stream, which starts near the Equator, where the water is warm, and flows north through the Atlantic Ocean towards Western Europe. (b) It is a warm current, carrying warm water from near the equator toward the poles; this warm water reaches the UK coast, and since currents affect the climate of coastal areas, the town is warmer than other places at the same latitude.
s: (a) The Gulf Stream, starting near the Equator
(b) As a warm current it brings warm water from the equator to the UK coast, and currents affect coastal climate

questions.q: In the chapter's table of smaller water bodies and waterways, the Strait of Malacca is the example given for one type. How does the table describe that type?
questions.a: A narrow channel joining two seas or oceans
o: A narrow channel joining two seas or oceans
A man-made channel connecting water bodies
A smaller, broad inlet of the sea
A large inlet of the sea deeply cutting into land

questions.q:
Match each type of water body in Column A with the example the chapter gives for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Sea 2. Gulf 3. Bay 4. Canal
Column B: P. Bay of Bengal Q. Suez Canal R. Arabian Sea S. Persian Gulf
(a) What is a reef? (b) Why are reefs often called the 'rainforests of the sea'?
questions.a: (a) A reef is a ridge found at or near the surface of the ocean, formed either naturally or artificially; natural reefs can be made of rock or built by tiny sea animals called corals. (b) Reefs are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth and provide food and shelter for about one-quarter of all ocean species, such as fish, crabs, turtles and sponges.
s: (a) A ridge at or near the ocean surface, formed naturally or artificially
(b) Among the most diverse ecosystems, giving food and shelter to about one-quarter of all ocean species

questions.q:
A shipping clerk in Mumbai writes a note for new staff in 2026: 'Our cargo ships bound for London leave Mumbai, cross the Arabian Sea and enter the Red Sea. They then pass through the Suez Canal, opened in 1869, into the Mediterranean. Before the canal existed, ships from India had to sail all the way around Africa to reach Europe.'
(a) How many years had the Suez Canal been open in 2026?
(b) Which two seas does the Suez Canal connect?
(c) Under the chapter's classification, is the Suez Canal a strait or a canal? Give the reason.
(d) Why do the firm's ships use the canal instead of sailing around Africa?
questions.a: (a) 2026 - 1869 = 157 years. (b) The Red Sea and the Mediterranean. (c) A canal, because it is a man-made channel connecting water bodies; a strait is a narrow channel joining two seas or oceans and is not described as man-made. (d) The Suez Canal is the shortest maritime route from India to Europe, creating a waterway from the Indian Ocean to Europe, so the voyage around Africa is avoided.
s: (a) 157 years
(b) The Red Sea and the Mediterranean
(c) A canal: a man-made channel connecting water bodies
(d) It is the shortest maritime route from India to Europe

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bays provide good places for ports and dockyards.
Reason (R): The Bay of Bengal is the world's largest bay.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A reef tour guide tells visitors: 'The Great Barrier Reef is safe for ever, because UNESCO has recognised it as a World Heritage Site.' Test the guide's claim using the chapter: (a) what the reef is home to, (b) the threats reefs face, and (c) what coral bleaching is caused by and what it does. Then give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) The reef, off Australia's northeastern coast, is a complex habitat of hundreds of species of coral and thousands of species of fish and other sea animals; its World Heritage status shows how remarkable it is. (b) But reefs face serious threats from human activities such as overfishing, pollution and climate change, which is why their conservation is crucial. (c) Coral bleaching happens because of changes in the chemical composition of ocean waters, largely caused by human actions, and the bleaching and death of coral takes away the habitat of a whole host of sea animals. Verdict: the claim is wrong; recognition shows the reef's value but does not remove the threats.
s: (a) Home to hundreds of coral species and thousands of fish and other sea animals; status shows its value
(b) Threatened by overfishing, pollution and climate change, so conservation is crucial
(c) Bleaching from human-caused changes in ocean chemistry destroys habitat; verdict: the claim is wrong

questions.q: True or False? 'The Persian Gulf is a gulf, not a bay, so it has played no part in trade between India and Europe.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. A gulf is a large inlet of the sea deeply cutting into land, and the chapter says the Persian Gulf has been important for trade between India and Europe for millennia.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Persian Gulf has been important for trade between India and Europe for millennia

questions.q: Which list gives the seven continents in the chapter's most common count?
questions.a: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America
o: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America
Africa, the Arctic, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, South America
Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Greenland, Europe, North America, South America
Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Eurasia, North America, South America

questions.q: (a) Using the chapter's definition, what is a plateau? (b) Name the highest and largest plateau on Earth.
questions.a: (a) A plateau is a landform that rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface; some of its sides are often steep slopes. (b) The Tibetan Plateau.
s: (a) Rises from the surrounding land with a more or less flat surface, some sides steep
(b) The Tibetan Plateau

questions.q: Answer these four short parts about the Tibetan Plateau using the chapter. (a) Collisions between which two tectonic plates formed it? (b) Which mountain range was formed by the same collisions? (c) Name three major rivers that have their source in the plateau. (d) The plateau stretches about 2,500 km from east to west and about 1,000 km from north to south. How many times its north-south extent is its east-west extent?
questions.a: (a) The Indo-Australian and Eurasian tectonic plates. (b) The Himalayan mountain range. (c) The Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Yangtze. (d) 2,500 / 1,000 = 2.5 times.
s: (a) The Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates
(b) The Himalayan range
(c) Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze

questions.q: A student compares two satellite pictures of the same part of the Tibetan Plateau, one taken in 1987 and one in 2021. Based on what the chapter says about climate change in the region, what is she most likely to notice in the 2021 picture?

Most lakes have dried up, because snow no longer melts on the plateau.
The plateau has become a plain with no steep sides left.

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'The Tibetan Plateau has an average height of over 4,500 metres, so it should really be called a mountain range, not a plateau.' Test his claim using the chapter's definitions of a mountain and a plateau and its description of the Tibetan Plateau, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Height alone does not decide the landform. A mountain is much higher than its surroundings with a broad base, steep slopes and a narrow summit. A plateau rises from the surrounding land and has a more or less flat surface, with some steep sides. The chapter describes the Tibetan Plateau as an expanse of flat land with the steep Himalayan mountains towards the south, and calls it the highest and largest plateau on Earth. Verdict: Ishaan is wrong; its great height makes it the highest plateau, not a mountain range.
s: States the mountain definition: broad base, steep slopes, narrow summit
States the plateau definition: rises from surrounding land, more or less flat surface, some steep sides
Applies it: the Tibetan Plateau is a flat expanse, the highest plateau; verdict, the claim is wrong

questions.q: A school geography club must choose ONE landform from the chapter's tour of Asia (the Tibetan Plateau, the Gobi Desert or the Eurasian Steppes) for a poster titled 'Asia's water bank'. Evaluate all three: give two facts on the Tibetan Plateau's link to water and climate, one fact on how water supports life in the Gobi, and one fact on what the Steppes do for the planet. Then make and justify the choice.
questions.a: Tibetan Plateau: it is the source of many major rivers, including the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze, and it contains the largest reserves of freshwater outside the polar regions, which is why it is called the Third Pole; it also influences the climate of Asia. Gobi: the climate is harsh and vegetation sparse, and herds migrate seasonally to pastures supported by underground water supplies; water there is scarce, not stored in bulk. Steppes: they are a global carbon sink that absorbs carbon from the air and stores it underground, and with nearby water bodies they are resting spots for migratory birds like the Siberian crane; their main value is carbon, not water. Choice: the Tibetan Plateau, because its freshwater reserves and the rivers it feeds make it the one landform of the three that truly works as Asia's store of water.
s: Tibetan Plateau: source of the Indus, Brahmaputra and Yangtze
Tibetan Plateau: largest freshwater reserves outside the polar regions (the Third Pole), influences Asia's climate
Gobi: sparse vegetation; herds migrate to pastures supported by underground water
Steppes: a global carbon sink, resting spot for migratory birds; value is carbon, not water
Choice: the Tibetan Plateau, justified by its freshwater and rivers

(b) At a height, they provide freshwater through melting snow and glaciers
(c) Europe and Asia

questions.q:
A clean-energy company wants to build a large solar farm in Mongolia and has two possible sites. Site P is at the edge of the Gobi Desert, where a weather station recorded 17 cm of precipitation last year. Site Q is on open steppe grassland, where the station recorded 32 cm (both figures illustrative). The company already knows that Mongolia has about 8 to 9 months of sunny weather a year, and that herders on both sites move their animals with the seasons.
(a) Using the chapter's precipitation limit, which site lies in a desert?
(b) For about how many months of the year does Mongolia NOT have sunny weather?
(c) Name one role the steppe grassland plays for the whole planet that clearing it for panels could harm.
(d) Which site should the company choose? Give one reason for your choice and one precaution the chapter's facts suggest.
questions.a: (a) Site P only, because 17 cm is less than the 25 cm a year that marks a desert, while 32 cm is more. (b) 12 - 9 = 3 to 12 - 8 = 4, so about 3 to 4 months. (c) The steppe grassland is a global carbon sink: it absorbs carbon from the air and stores it underground, which helps reduce greenhouse effects; its water bodies are also resting spots for migratory birds like the Siberian crane. (d) Site P: the Gobi's vegetation is sparse and the sky is sunny for 8 to 9 months, and the chapter shows solar panels already harnessing energy there, so less of value is lost than by clearing a carbon-sink grassland. Precaution: herds in the Gobi migrate seasonally to pastures supported by underground water, so the farm must not block those routes or damage the water supply.
s: (a) Site P, since 17 cm is below the 25 cm desert limit
(b) About 3 to 4 months
(c) The steppe is a global carbon sink (or a resting spot for migratory birds such as the Siberian crane)
(d) Chooses Site P with a reason (sparse vegetation, long sunny season, keeps the carbon sink) and a precaution for seasonal herds and underground water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Eurasian Steppes help to reduce greenhouse effects over time.
Reason (R): The Eurasian Steppes are a dense coniferous forest that absorbs carbon through its trees.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: The chapter quotes the National Geographic Society: around one billion people, one-eighth of the world's population, live in deserts. (a) What total world population do these two figures together imply? (b) A classmate says, 'Deserts cover about one-fifth of the Earth's land, so one-fifth of all people live in deserts.' Correct her.
questions.a: (a) 1 billion x 8 = about 8 billion people. (b) She has mixed up two figures: one-fifth is the share of the Earth's land area that deserts cover, but the share of people living in deserts is one-eighth, about one billion.
s: (a) 1 billion x 8 = about 8 billion
(b) One-fifth is the land area; the share of people living in deserts is one-eighth

Match each item in Column A with the correct examples from the chapter in Column B.

Column B: P. Iron, copper, lead and rock salt Q. Moscow, Berlin, Paris and Warsaw R. The Rhine and tributaries of the Danube S. Wheat, barley, rye and potatoes
(a) What does the chapter say has happened on the European Plain because many rulers wanted to control it? (b) For which two activities does the European Plain remain vital to Europe's economy today?
questions.a: (a) The European Plain has been the ground for major battles, with many rulers jostling to take control of it. (b) Agriculture and transportation.
s: (a) It has been the ground for major battles
(b) Agriculture and transportation

questions.q: A European business group plans five projects and must place each one either on the European Plain or in the Alps. For each project, choose the region and give the fact from the chapter that supports your choice. (a) A flour mill that needs a steady supply of wheat. (b) A mine for graphite and rock salt. (c) A company that carries goods by river barge. (d) A ski and hiking resort. (e) A power station that runs on coal or natural gas mined nearby.
questions.a: (a) The European Plain: its fertile soils make it one of the most productive farming regions, and wheat is widely grown there. (b) The Alps: they are rich in minerals such as graphite and rock salt (with iron, copper, lead, gypsum and magnesite). (c) The European Plain: its rivers have played an important role in trade and transport. (d) The Alps: they are renowned for skiing and hiking in all the countries they span. (e) The European Plain: it has deposits of coal, oil and natural gas.
s: (a) European Plain: fertile soils, wheat widely grown
(b) Alps: rich in graphite and rock salt
(c) European Plain: its rivers are important for trade and transport
(d) Alps: known for skiing and hiking
(e) European Plain: deposits of coal, oil and natural gas

questions.q: A photograph caption in the chapter says that the largest proportion of the world's wheat production is from Europe. Which feature of the European Plain, as the chapter describes it, best accounts for this?
questions.a: Fertile soils on flat land formed by sediment deposition
o: Fertile soils on flat land formed by sediment deposition
Deposits of coal, oil and natural gas under the plain
Its history as the ground for major battles
Oak and beech forests on its lower slopes

questions.q: Kabir says: 'The European Plain and the Alps are completely different. One is flat farmland and the other is a wall of high peaks, so neither is of any use to the other.' Test both parts of Kabir's claim using the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: First part, right: the European Plain is low-lying, flat land with gentle rolling hills and wide river valleys, while the Alps are a crescent-shaped mountain range that forms a natural barrier with peaks such as Mont Blanc. Second part, wrong: the Alps provide water to major rivers such as the Rhine and the tributaries of the Danube, which supply drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power to lowland Europe. Verdict: partly right; the two look different, but the mountains feed the water that the plain's farms and towns use.
s: First part right: the plain is low-lying flat land, the Alps a crescent-shaped mountain barrier
Second part wrong: the Alps feed the Rhine and Danube tributaries that give lowland Europe water, irrigation and hydroelectric power
Verdict: partly right

questions.a: A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a savannah? (b) Name two animals of the African savannah that depend on its grasses and waterholes.
questions.a: (a) A savannah is a tropical grassland ecosystem with wide open spaces, scattered trees and seasonal rainfall. (b) Any two of: elephants, lions, zebras, giraffes.

questions.q: The chapter says temperatures across the Sahara range from 30 degrees Celsius to 46 degrees Celsius, and that its plants and animals have adapted to heat sometimes upward of 50 degrees Celsius. (a) By how many degrees do the Sahara's temperatures range? (b) By how many degrees does 50 degrees Celsius exceed the top of that range? (c) Using the fennec fox, show one way an animal copes with such heat.
questions.a: (a) 46 - 30 = 16 degrees Celsius. (b) 50 - 46 = 4 degrees Celsius. (c) The Saharan fennec fox has large ears that help it dissipate heat (they also help it listen for underground prey).

(b) 50 - 46 = 4 degrees Celsius

questions.q: A documentary team on northern Africa must decide its title: 'Life shaped by the Sahara' or 'Life shaped by the Nile'. Evaluate the evidence: (a) state the Sahara's rainfall and vegetation; (b) describe how nomadic people earn a living there; (c) say what the ancient trade routes through it carried; (d) describe three uses the Nile serves for people; (e) choose a title and justify it using your answers.
questions.a: (a) The Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world, has rainfall below 25 cm and hardly any vegetation. (b) Nomadic tribes herd sheep, goats and camels and engage in trade for their livelihood. (c) Ancient trade routes carried gold, salt and ideas to the Mediterranean world. (d) Any three: the Nile provides irrigation that turns dry lands into fertile farmland for wheat, barley, flax, fruits and vegetables; drinking water; fishing; hydroelectric power; and a transportation route; its basin was the cradle of the ancient Egyptian civilisation. (e) A justified choice, for example 'Life shaped by the Nile', because the river turns desert into farmland and supports settled life on a large scale, while the Sahara supports mainly herding and passing trade; a choice of the Sahara title is acceptable if justified by the herding and long-distance trade it shaped.
s: (a) Rainfall below 25 cm, hardly any vegetation
(b) Nomads herd sheep, goats and camels and trade
(c) Routes carried gold, salt and ideas to the Mediterranean world
(d) Three Nile uses: irrigation for crops, drinking water, fishing, hydroelectric power, transport
(e) A title chosen and justified from the evidence in (a) to (d)

questions.q:
An irrigation officer studies a village beside the Nile that has 400 hectares of land (illustrative figures). Before new irrigation channels were dug, only 120 hectares could be farmed; now 340 hectares are farmed. The village also has fishing families, and boats carry its harvest along the river. A company now proposes a small dam upstream for hydroelectric power, which would lower the river for some weeks a year.
(a) By how many hectares has the farmed area grown?
(b) What percentage of the village's land is now farmed?
(c) Name two crops the chapter says Nile irrigation supports.
(d) Should the village support the dam? Weigh one benefit against one cost using the uses of the Nile the chapter lists.
questions.a: (a) 340 - 120 = 220 hectares. (b) 340 / 400 x 100 = 85 per cent. (c) Any two of: wheat, barley, flax, fruits, vegetables. (d) A weighed judgement: hydroelectric power is one of the uses the chapter lists for the Nile, so the dam brings electricity; but the Nile also gives irrigation, fishing and a transport route, and a lower river for some weeks could hurt the fishing families, the boats carrying the harvest and the irrigated fields. The village could support it only if water for irrigation, fishing and boats is protected in those weeks, or oppose it if it cannot be.
s: (a) 220 hectares
(b) 85 per cent
(c) Any two of wheat, barley, flax, fruits, vegetables
(d) Weighs hydroelectric power against the river's irrigation, fishing and transport uses and gives a conditional decision

questions.q:
Match each need in the Sahara in Column A with what the chapter shows meeting it in Column B.

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What is a salt flat, and in which country is the largest salt flat on Earth? (b) From which mountains does the Amazon River flow, and towards which ocean? (c) About how many indigenous communities live in the Amazon Rainforest?
questions.a: (a) A salt flat is an area of flat land covered with a layer of salt; the largest on Earth, the Uyuni Salt Flats, is in Bolivia. (b) It flows from the Andes Mountains in Peru east towards the Atlantic Ocean. (c) Almost 400.
s: (a) Flat land covered with a layer of salt; the largest is in Bolivia (Uyuni)
(b) From the Andes, east towards the Atlantic Ocean
(c) Almost 400

questions.q: A student is making a two-column chart titled 'One continent, two extremes' that sets the Amazon Rainforest beside the Atacama Desert. Fill it in four steps: (a) describe each place's rainfall and vegetation; (b) give one fact about the size or temperature of the Atacama; (c) name the people who help conserve the Amazon and their role; (d) give the main human-made threat to each place.
questions.a: (a) The Amazon Rainforest is an area of tall, mostly evergreen trees that receives a high amount of rainfall; the Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth. (b) The Atacama stretches about 1,000 km, and its temperature varies from 40 degrees Celsius during the day to 5 degrees Celsius at night. (c) Almost 400 indigenous communities live in the Amazon forest and play an important role in conserving it. (d) The Amazon is threatened by deforestation and climate change; the Atacama has become one of the world's fastest-growing dumps for discarded clothes from cheap fast fashion, which the UN calls an environmental and social emergency.
s: (a) Amazon: tall, mostly evergreen trees, high rainfall; Atacama: one of the driest places
(b) Atacama: about 1,000 km long, or 40 degrees Celsius by day and 5 degrees Celsius at night
(c) Almost 400 indigenous communities who help conserve the forest
(d) Amazon: deforestation and climate change; Atacama: fast-fashion clothing dumps

questions.q:
Illustrative figures for a mountain park (not from the book): the park held about 20,000 elk, and survey plots showed on average 3 young willow plants each, because the elk ate almost every shoot. Wolves were brought in, as at Yellowstone. Ten years later the park held about 12,000 elk and the plots showed on average 15 young willows each. A cattle rancher next to the park now asks for the wolves to be removed, fearing for his herd.
(a) What problem did Yellowstone face before wolves were introduced?
(b) By what percentage did the park's elk population fall?
(c) Explain the rise in young willows using the chapter's chain of events.
(d) Should the park remove the wolves? Give a judgement that weighs the rancher's fear against the park's balance.
questions.a: (a) An ecological imbalance caused by overgrazing by elk, a type of deer. (b) (20,000 - 12,000) / 20,000 x 100 = 40 per cent. (c) The wolves, as predators, hunted the elk and reduced their number, so fewer shoots were eaten and the plants (flora) returned, restoring the balance as at Yellowstone. (d) A weighed judgement: removing the wolves would let the elk multiply and overgraze again, undoing the 5-fold rise in willows; but the rancher's herd is a real concern, so the park should keep the wolves and protect his cattle by other means, such as secure fencing or compensation for losses.
s: (a) Overgrazing by elk caused an ecological imbalance
(b) 40 per cent
(c) Wolves hunted elk, fewer shoots eaten, flora returned
(d) A judgement that weighs the rancher's fear against the risk of overgrazing returning

questions.q: Compare the Rocky Mountains and the Appalachian Mountains of North America on four points: (a) the resources each provides; (b) the indigenous communities linked to each and how they relate to the mountains; (c) what has happened to the Rockies' indigenous communities; (d) the sectors that drive or are growing in each range's economy. (e) Then judge which of the two ranges the chapter shows moving most clearly toward newer sectors, and support your judgement with evidence.
questions.a: (a) The Rockies are rich in copper, gold and silver; the Appalachians provide coal, timber and natural gas. (b) The Rockies were home to large Native American communities, who depended on the rivers, forests and wildlife and regarded the mountains as sacred; in the Appalachians, fertile valleys, abundant game and natural travel routes let indigenous communities such as the Cherokee thrive, and the mountains hold spiritual significance for them. (c) The large communities of the Rockies lived there till about 300 years ago; today many of them live on reservations established for them. (d) In the Rockies, mining, hydropower generation, tourism and agriculture contribute to the GDP; in the Appalachians, coal, timber and natural gas industries have been vital, while tourism and renewable energy are growing sectors. (e) The Appalachians: the chapter names tourism and renewable energy as growing sectors there, beside the older coal, timber and natural gas industries, while for the Rockies it lists mining, hydropower, tourism and agriculture as present contributors without naming any as growing.
s: (a) Rockies: copper, gold, silver; Appalachians: coal, timber, natural gas
(b) Native Americans of the Rockies held the mountains sacred; the Cherokee of the Appalachians thrived on valleys, game and routes
(c) The Rockies' communities lived there till about 300 years ago and many now live on reservations
(d) Rockies: mining, hydropower, tourism, agriculture; Appalachians: tourism and renewable energy growing
(e) Judges the Appalachians, citing tourism and renewable energy as growing sectors beside coal, timber and gas

questions.q: Ravi says: 'A desert must be hot and sandy, so icy Antarctica cannot be a desert at all, let alone the largest one on Earth.' Test Ravi's claim using what the chapter says decides a desert, its examples of cold deserts, and its facts on Antarctica, and give your verdict.
questions.a: A desert is decided by dryness, not heat: deserts are large, extremely dry areas of land with low precipitation, less than 25 cm a year. The chapter says there are cold deserts too, such as the Gobi in Asia. Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth, covering over 14 million square kilometres, more than four times the area of India, and it is the coldest desert, even colder than the Arctic, the planet's other polar desert. Verdict: Ravi is wrong.
s: A desert is defined by low precipitation (less than 25 cm a year), not by heat
Cold deserts exist, for example the Gobi
Antarctica is the largest (over 14 million sq km) and coldest desert; verdict, the claim is wrong
